items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A phase in which particles vibrate about fixed positions and are held close together by strong intermolecular forces"?
items.answer: solid (particle model)
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of solid (particle model).

items.stem: Amara writes: "Particles in a solid do not move." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: They vibrate continuously about fixed equilibrium positions; their kinetic energy increases with temperature.
items.markingKey: They vibrate continuously about fixed equilibrium positions; their kinetic energy increases with temperature. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A teacher in Mexico City asks a class to choose the one correct statement about molecular theory of solids, liquids and gases; density. Which statement should be chosen?
options: When a substance expands, its particles get bigger.
The particles stay the same size; the mean spacing between them increases.
Cold objects do not emit any radiation.
items.answer: The particles stay the same size; the mean spacing between them increases.
items.markingKey: B. The other options are common misconceptions. The particles stay the same size; the mean spacing between them increases.

items.stem: Liquid water has a density of 1000 kg m⁻³ and its vapour, under certain conditions, has a density of 0.8 kg m⁻³. Estimate the ratio of mean molecular spacing in the vapour to that in the liquid.
Liquid mercury has a density of 13600 kg m⁻³ and its vapour, under certain conditions, has a density of 1.2 kg m⁻³. Estimate the ratio of mean molecular spacing in the vapour to that in the liquid.
Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "The simple particle model is sufficient to explain all the properties of matter."
items.answer: The model is powerful for many thermal properties, but more detailed models of bonding and quantum behaviour are needed (NOS: models have limitations).
items.markingKey: Arguments for: explains density differences, compressibility, diffusion and thermal expansion. Arguments against: does not explain water’s density anomaly without hydrogen bonding; cannot explain electrical conductivity or magnetism; quantum effects matter at low temperatures (superfluids). Supported judgement: The model is powerful for many thermal properties, but more detailed models of bonding and quantum behaviour are needed (NOS: models have limitations).

items.stem: What is the density of water in kg m⁻³?
items.answer: 1000 kg m⁻³
items.markingKey: A. 1 g cm⁻³.

items.stem: Diffusion is faster in gases than in liquids because gas particles
options: move faster and have larger spacing, so they travel further between collisions
items.answer: move faster and have larger spacing, so they travel further between collisions
items.markingKey: C. Mean free path is longer.

items.stem: Explain why ice floats on water.
items.answer: Hydrogen bonding holds water molecules in an open lattice in ice, so ice is less dense (≈ 917 kg m⁻³) than liquid water; the upthrust exceeds its weight when fully submerged.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Hydrogen bonding holds water molecules in an open lattice in ice, so ice is less dense (≈ 917 kg m⁻³) than liquid water; the upthrust exceeds its weight when fully submerged. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between the arrangement of particles in a gas and the arrangement of particles in a solid.
items.answer: In a solid, particles are closely packed in fixed positions and vibrate; in a gas, they are far apart (≈ 10 diameters) and move freely and randomly with negligible forces between collisions.
items.markingKey: In a solid, particles are closely packed in fixed positions and vibrate; in a gas, they are far apart (≈ 10 diameters) and move freely and randomly with negligible forces between collisions. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Heavy objects are always dense." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Density is mass per unit volume; a large, heavy object such as a ship can have a low average density.
items.markingKey: Density is mass per unit volume; a large, heavy object such as a ship can have a low average density. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Liquid ethanol has a density of 789 kg m⁻³ and its vapour, under certain conditions, has a density of 0.6 kg m⁻³. Estimate the ratio of mean molecular spacing in the vapour to that in the liquid.
A classroom in Accra measures 10 m × 8 m × 3.0 m. The density of air is 1.2 kg m⁻³. Calculate the mass of air in the room.
items.answer: 288 kg

items.stem: An irregular stone is lowered into a measuring cylinder containing 50.0 cm³ of water; the level rises to 68.5 cm³. The stone has a mass of 49.1 g. (a) Calculate the density of the stone in kg m⁻³. (b) The volume readings have an uncertainty of ±0.5 cm³ and the mass ±0.1 g. Determine the percentage uncertainty in the density. (c) Suggest one improvement to the method. (d) Identify whether the stone would float in mercury (13 600 kg m⁻³).
items.answer: (a) V = 18.5 cm³, ρ = 2.65 g cm⁻³ = 2650 kg m⁻³; (b) ΔV = 1.0 cm³ (two readings) → 5.4 %, mass 0.2 %, total ≈ 5.6 %; (c) use a displacement (eureka) can with a narrower cylinder or a density balance; (d) yes – its density is less than mercury’s.
items.markingKey: (a) V = 18.5 cm³, ρ = 2.65 g cm⁻³ = 2650 kg m⁻³; (b) ΔV = 1.0 cm³ (two readings) → 5.4 %, mass 0.2 %, total ≈ 5.6 %; (c) use a displacement (eureka) can with a narrower cylinder or a density balance; (d) yes – its density is less than mercury’s.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The total random kinetic energy and intermolecular potential energy of the particles in a substance"?
items.answer: internal energy
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of internal energy.

items.stem: A student claims: "An object at 0 °C contains no internal energy." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: 0 °C is 273 K; its particles still have kinetic and potential energy. Only at absolute zero is the kinetic energy at a minimum.
items.markingKey: 0 °C is 273 K; its particles still have kinetic and potential energy. Only at absolute zero is the kinetic energy at a minimum. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A teacher in Mexico City asks a class to choose the one correct statement about temperature, internal energy and specific heat capacity. Which statement should be chosen?
options: An object at 0 °C contains no internal energy.
A hotter black body emits less at long wavelengths than a cooler one.
Heat and temperature are the same thing.
Temperature measures average particle kinetic energy; heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference.
items.answer: Temperature measures average particle kinetic energy; heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference.
items.markingKey: D. The other options are common misconceptions. Temperature measures average particle kinetic energy; heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference.

items.stem: Calculate the energy needed to raise the temperature of 3.5 kg of concrete (c = 880 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) by 8 K.

Tomás repeated a method-of-mixtures experiment with hot copper and cold water. The 5 readings of the final temperature of the water were 31.0, 30.3, 31.5, 30.8, 30.4 °C. Determine the mean, the absolute uncertainty and the percentage uncertainty, and state the result to an appropriate number of significant figures.
items.markingKey: Mean = 30.8 °C (A1); absolute uncertainty = half range = 0.6 °C (A1); percentage uncertainty = 0.6/30.8 × 100 = 1.9 % (A1). Result quoted to the same decimal place as the uncertainty.

items.stem: 0.4 kg of water at 90 °C is mixed with 0.1 kg of water at 20 °C in an insulated flask. Calculate the final temperature.
items.markingKey: A. Energy lost = energy gained: 0.4c(90 − T) = 0.1c(T − 20) (M1); T = 76.0 °C (A1).

items.stem:
A 1.00 kg aluminium block is heated by a 48.0 W heater. The temperature θ is recorded every minute. Theory (no losses): Pt = mc(θ − θ₀).

t / s | θ / °C
60 | 23.0
120 | 26.1
180 | 29.1
240 | 32.2
300 | 35.3
360 | 38.0

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the specific heat capacity c of aluminium. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±5 %. State c with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) θ (y) against t (x); (b) gradient ≈ 0.0503 K s⁻¹; (c) 954 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; (d) (950 ± 50) J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) θ (y) against t (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 0.0503 K s⁻¹ – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) c = P/(m × gradient) = 954 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 5 % of the value = 50 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem: A 1.20 kg aluminium block is heated by a 50.0 W immersion heater for 6.00 min; its temperature rises from 20.5 °C to 35.8 °C. (a) Calculate the energy supplied. (b) Determine the specific heat capacity of aluminium from the data. (c) The accepted value is 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; calculate the percentage difference and suggest the main reason. (d) Describe two improvements.
items.answer: (a) 18 000 J; (b) c = 18 000/(1.20 × 15.3) = 980 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; (c) 8.9 % high – energy lost to the surroundings; (d) insulate the block (lagging), put oil in the thermometer and heater holes, start below room temperature and finish the same amount above it.
items.markingKey: (a) 18 000 J; (b) c = 18 000/(1.20 × 15.3) = 980 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; (c) 8.9 % high – energy lost to the surroundings; (d) insulate the block (lagging), put oil in the thermometer and heater holes, start below room temperature and finish the same amount above it.

items.stem: What temperature in kelvin corresponds to 27 °C?
Which of the following best describes "internal energy"?
options: Energy transferred from a region of higher temperature to one of lower temperature
The model in which matter is made of particles in constant random motion whose average kinetic energy depends on temperature
An idealised object that absorbs all incident radiation and emits the maximum possible radiation at each wavelength for its temperature
The total random kinetic energy and intermolecular potential energy of the particles in a substance
items.answer: The total random kinetic energy and intermolecular potential energy of the particles in a substance
items.markingKey: D. "internal energy" is the total random kinetic energy and intermolecular potential energy of the particles in a substance.

items.stem: The temperature of a gas in kelvin doubles. The mean kinetic energy of its molecules
items.answer: doubles
items.markingKey: D. Eₖ ∝ T.

items.stem: Distinguish between internal energy and temperature.
items.answer: Temperature is related to the average random kinetic energy per particle; internal energy is the total random kinetic plus intermolecular potential energy of all the particles, so it also depends on the amount and phase of the substance.
items.markingKey: Temperature is related to the average random kinetic energy per particle; internal energy is the total random kinetic plus intermolecular potential energy of all the particles, so it also depends on the amount and phase of the substance. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
This question is about temperature, internal energy and specific heat capacity.

(a) Ana repeated a method-of-mixtures experiment with hot copper and cold water. The 5 readings of the final temperature of the water were 31.4, 31.5, 31.3, 31.3, 31.4 °C. Determine the mean, the absolute uncertainty and the percentage uncertainty, and state the result to an appropriate number of significant figures. [3]

(b) Distinguish between internal energy and temperature. [4]

(c) Evaluate the claim: "Water’s high specific heat capacity is the main reason Earth’s climate is habitable." [4]
items.answer: (a) 31.4 ± 0.1 °C (0.3 %) (b) Temperature is related to the average random kinetic energy per particle; internal energy is the total random kinetic plus intermolecular potential energy of all the particles, so it also depends on the amount and phase of the substance. (c) Water’s heat capacity is a key moderating factor, but habitability depends on a combination of energy balance, the greenhouse effect and the water cycle.
items.markingKey: (a) [3 marks] Mean = 31.4 °C (A1); absolute uncertainty = half range = 0.1 °C (A1); percentage uncertainty = 0.1/31.4 × 100 = 0.3 % (A1). Result quoted to the same decimal place as the uncertainty. (b) [4 marks] Temperature is related to the average random kinetic energy per particle; internal energy is the total random kinetic plus intermolecular potential energy of all the particles, so it also depends on the amount and phase of the substance. (c) [4 marks] For: oceans store huge amounts of energy, moderating temperature swings; ocean currents redistribute energy from equator to poles. Against: the greenhouse effect and atmospheric composition are also essential; distance from the Sun and albedo determine the overall temperature; water vapour and clouds also matter. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: Water’s heat capacity is a key moderating factor, but habitability depends on a combination of energy balance, the greenhouse effect and the water cycle.

items.answer: Water’s heat capacity is a key moderating factor, but habitability depends on a combination of energy balance, the greenhouse effect and the water cycle.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: oceans store huge amounts of energy, moderating temperature swings; ocean currents redistribute energy from equator to poles. Arguments against: the greenhouse effect and atmospheric composition are also essential; distance from the Sun and albedo determine the overall temperature; water vapour and clouds also matter. Supported judgement: Water’s heat capacity is a key moderating factor, but habitability depends on a combination of energy balance, the greenhouse effect and the water cycle. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The energy required to change 1 kg of a substance from solid to liquid without a change in temperature"?
items.answer: specific latent heat of fusion
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of specific latent heat of fusion.

items.stem: Why does blowing across hot soup cool it faster?
options: It adds cold air molecules to the soup
It decreases the specific heat capacity
It removes vapour, increasing the rate of evaporation
items.answer: It removes vapour, increasing the rate of evaporation
items.markingKey: D. Evaporation carries away latent heat.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about phase change and specific latent heat is a common misconception? (Revision quiz set by Elena.)
options: A hotter black body emits more at every wavelength; its peak simply moves to shorter wavelengths.
Adding more heat to boiling water makes it hotter.
Average kinetic energy is proportional to absolute temperature; 20 °C → 40 °C is 293 K → 313 K, an increase of only about 7 %.
The particles stay the same size; the mean spacing between them increases.
items.answer: Adding more heat to boiling water makes it hotter.
items.markingKey: B. This is incorrect: The temperature stays at the boiling point; extra power only makes it boil away faster.

items.stem: Calculate the total energy needed to turn 0.1 kg of water at 25 °C completely into steam at 100 °C.
items.markingKey: C. Heating: 3.14 × 10⁴ J (M1); vaporizing: 2.26 × 10⁵ J (M1); total 2.57 × 10⁵ J (A1).

items.stem: Calculate the total energy needed to turn 0.5 kg of water at 20 °C completely into steam at 100 °C.
items.markingKey: Heating: 1.67 × 10⁵ J (M1); vaporizing: 1.13 × 10⁶ J (M1); total 1.30 × 10⁶ J (A1).

items.stem:
This question is about phase change and specific latent heat.

(a) Calculate the total energy needed to turn 0.1 kg of water at 25 °C completely into steam at 100 °C. [3]

(b) Explain the difference between boiling and evaporation. [4]

(c) Evaluate the claim: "Ice packs are more effective than cold water packs of the same mass and temperature for treating sports injuries." [4]
items.answer: (a) 2.57 × 10⁵ J (b) Evaporation occurs only at the surface and at any temperature, with the most energetic molecules escaping; boiling occurs throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature (for a given pressure), with bubbles of vapour forming. (c) Ice absorbs far more energy per kilogram because of latent heat, so it cools longer, though care and comfort matter in practice.
items.markingKey: (a) [3 marks] Heating: 3.14 × 10⁴ J (M1); vaporizing: 2.26 × 10⁵ J (M1); total 2.57 × 10⁵ J (A1). (b) [4 marks] Evaporation occurs only at the surface and at any temperature, with the most energetic molecules escaping; boiling occurs throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature (for a given pressure), with bubbles of vapour forming. (c) [4 marks] For: melting ice absorbs 334 kJ kg⁻¹ at constant 0 °C; keeps a steady low temperature for longer. Against: ice can damage skin if applied directly; gel packs offer flexibility; cold water is easier to control and less extreme. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: Ice absorbs far more energy per kilogram because of latent heat, so it cools longer, though care and comfort matter in practice.

items.stem: During melting, the temperature of a pure substance
items.answer: stays constant
items.markingKey: D. Energy goes into breaking bonds (potential energy).

items.stem: Briefly explain why a scald from steam at 100 °C is more severe than one from water at 100 °C.
items.answer: Steam condensing on the skin releases its large latent heat of vaporization (2.26 MJ kg⁻¹) in addition to the energy released as the water cools.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Steam condensing on the skin releases its large latent heat of vaporization (2.26 MJ kg⁻¹) in addition to the energy released as the water cools. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A 0.250 kg block of ice at −15.0 °C is placed in a kettle and heated until all of it has become steam at 100 °C. c(ice) = 2100 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, c(water) = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, L_f = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹, L_v = 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. (a) Sketch the temperature–time graph. (b) Calculate the energy for each stage and the total. (c) Explain why the boiling stage lasts much longer than the melting stage. (d) The kettle supplies 2.0 kW; estimate the total time.
items.answer: (a) rise, flat at 0 °C, rise, flat at 100 °C; (b) 7.9 kJ + 83.5 kJ + 104.5 kJ + 565 kJ = 761 kJ; (c) L_v is about 6.8 times L_f; (d) 380 s (longer in practice owing to losses).

items.stem: If the absolute temperature of a black body doubles, its radiated power
items.answer: increases by a factor of 16
items.markingKey: B. P ∝ T⁴.

items.stem: A teacher in Hanoi asks a class to choose the one correct statement about conduction, convection and thermal radiation; Stefan-Boltzmann law and Wien's law. Which statement should be chosen?
options: An object at 0 °C contains no internal energy.
Hot fluid rises because it is less dense; thermal energy itself can be transferred in any direction (e.g. conduction downwards, radiation).
Heat and temperature are the same thing.
When a substance expands, its particles get bigger.
items.answer: Hot fluid rises because it is less dense; thermal energy itself can be transferred in any direction (e.g. conduction downwards, radiation).
items.markingKey: B. The other options are common misconceptions. Hot fluid rises because it is less dense; thermal energy itself can be transferred in any direction (e.g. conduction downwards, radiation).

items.stem: Explain how convection currents form above a radiator.
items.answer: Air next to the radiator is heated, expands and becomes less dense, so it rises; cooler, denser air sinks to replace it, setting up a circulating current.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Air next to the radiator is heated, expands and becomes less dense, so it rises; cooler, denser air sinks to replace it, setting up a circulating current. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Nia writes: "A hotter black body emits less at long wavelengths than a cooler one." Explain why this is inaccurate.

T / K | P / W

(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the emissivity e of the plate. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±3 %. State e with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) P (y) against T⁴ (x); (b) gradient ≈ 5.33 × 10⁻¹⁰ W K⁻⁴; (c) 0.940; (d) 0.94 ± 0.03
items.markingKey: (a) P (y) against T⁴ (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 5.33 × 10⁻¹⁰ W K⁻⁴ – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) e = gradient/(σA) = 0.940 (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 3 % of the value = 0.03; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem:
This question is about conduction, convection and thermal radiation; Stefan-Boltzmann law and Wien's law.

(a) A star has a surface temperature of 25000 K. Calculate the wavelength at which its emission peaks. [2]

(b) Distinguish between convection and conduction. [4]

(c) Outline one argument for and one against the statement: "Insulating the loft is always the most cost-effective way to reduce a house’s heating bill." [4]
items.answer: (a) 1.16 × 10⁻⁷ m (b) Conduction transfers energy through collisions between particles (and free electrons) without bulk movement; convection transfers energy by bulk movement of a fluid driven by density differences. (c) Loft insulation is often the cheapest first step, but the best choice depends on the house; a survey of where energy is lost should guide decisions.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] λ_max = 2.9 × 10⁻³/T (M1) = 1.16 × 10⁻⁷ m (A1). (b) [4 marks] Conduction transfers energy through collisions between particles (and free electrons) without bulk movement; convection transfers energy by bulk movement of a fluid driven by density differences. (c) [4 marks] For: about a quarter of heat is lost through an uninsulated roof; loft insulation is cheap with a short payback time. Against: draughts, walls and windows may be bigger losses in some houses; already-insulated lofts have diminishing returns; heat-pump installation can reduce bills further. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: Loft insulation is often the cheapest first step, but the best choice depends on the house; a survey of where energy is lost should guide decisions.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "conduction".
items.answer: The transfer of thermal energy through a material by collisions between neighbouring particles and, in metals, by free electrons
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the transfer of thermal energy through a material by collisions between neighbouring particles and, in metals, by free electrons. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon have been in a drawer at the same temperature. The metal spoon feels colder because
options: it conducts thermal energy away from the hand faster
it is at a lower temperature
items.answer: it conducts thermal energy away from the hand faster
items.markingKey: A. Same temperature, higher conductivity.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a real surface with emissivity e < 1 and a black body.
items.answer: A black body absorbs all radiation and emits the maximum σAT⁴; a real surface emits only eσAT⁴ and reflects or transmits some incident radiation.
items.markingKey: A black body absorbs all radiation and emits the maximum σAT⁴; a real surface emits only eσAT⁴ and reflects or transmits some incident radiation. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A sheet of fibreglass insulation (thermal conductivity 0.04 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹) has area 1.0 m² and thickness 200 mm. Its faces are at a temperature difference of 10 K. Calculate the rate of thermal energy transfer by conduction.

items.stem: "Insulating the loft is always the most cost-effective way to reduce a house’s heating bill." Discuss.
items.answer: Loft insulation is often the cheapest first step, but the best choice depends on the house; a survey of where energy is lost should guide decisions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: about a quarter of heat is lost through an uninsulated roof; loft insulation is cheap with a short payback time. items.stem: Distinguish between convection and conduction.
items.answer: Conduction transfers energy through collisions between particles (and free electrons) without bulk movement; convection transfers energy by bulk movement of a fluid driven by density differences.

items.stem: Explain why the measured specific heat capacity of a metal block in a school experiment is usually higher than the true value.
items.answer: Energy is lost to the surroundings and to the heater and thermometer, so more energy is supplied than goes into the block, giving c = Q/(mΔT) too large.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Energy is lost to the surroundings and to the heater and thermometer, so more energy is supplied than goes into the block, giving c = Q/(mΔT) too large. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student in Bogotá is checking notes on molecular theory of solids, liquids and gases; density. Which statement is incorrect?

items.answer: Heavy objects are always dense.

items.stem: A student in Seoul is checking notes on phase change and specific latent heat. Which statement is incorrect?

items.stem:
This question is about temperature, internal energy and specific heat capacity.

(a) Jonas repeated a method-of-mixtures experiment with hot copper and cold water. The 5 readings of the final temperature of the water were 34.3, 36.0, 34.5, 36.7, 36.8 °C. Determine the mean, the absolute uncertainty and the percentage uncertainty, and state the result to an appropriate number of significant figures. [3]

(b) Explain the difference between temperature and internal energy. [4]

(c) Outline one argument for and one against the statement: "Water’s high specific heat capacity is the main reason Earth’s climate is habitable." [4]
items.answer: (a) 35.7 ± 1.2 °C (3.5 %) (b) Temperature is related to the average random kinetic energy per particle; internal energy is the total random kinetic plus intermolecular potential energy of all the particles, so it also depends on the amount and phase of the substance. (c) Water’s heat capacity is a key moderating factor, but habitability depends on a combination of energy balance, the greenhouse effect and the water cycle.
items.markingKey: (a) [3 marks] Mean = 35.7 °C (A1); absolute uncertainty = half range = 1.2 °C (A1); percentage uncertainty = 1.2/35.7 × 100 = 3.5 % (A1). Result quoted to the same decimal place as the uncertainty. (b) [4 marks] Temperature is related to the average random kinetic energy per particle; internal energy is the total random kinetic plus intermolecular potential energy of all the particles, so it also depends on the amount and phase of the substance. (c) [4 marks] For: oceans store huge amounts of energy, moderating temperature swings; ocean currents redistribute energy from equator to poles. Against: the greenhouse effect and atmospheric composition are also essential; distance from the Sun and albedo determine the overall temperature; water vapour and clouds also matter. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: Water’s heat capacity is a key moderating factor, but habitability depends on a combination of energy balance, the greenhouse effect and the water cycle.

items.stem:
This question is about molecular theory of solids, liquids and gases; density.

(a) Liquid mercury has a density of 13600 kg m⁻³ and its vapour, under certain conditions, has a density of 1.2 kg m⁻³. Estimate the ratio of mean molecular spacing in the vapour to that in the liquid. [2]

(b) With the help of a specific example, explain, using the particle model, why gases are easily compressed but liquids are not. [3]

(c) Evaluate the claim: "The simple particle model is sufficient to explain all the properties of matter." [4]
items.answer: (a) 22.5 (b) Gas particles are far apart with mostly empty space, so they can be pushed closer; in liquids the particles are already in contact and strong repulsive forces resist compression. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (c) The model is powerful for many thermal properties, but more detailed models of bonding and quantum behaviour are needed (NOS: models have limitations).
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] Spacing ∝ (1/ρ)^⅓ (M1); ratio = (13600/1.2)^⅓ = 22.5 (A1). (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (c) [4 marks] For: explains density differences, compressibility, diffusion and thermal expansion. Against: does not explain water’s density anomaly without hydrogen bonding; cannot explain electrical conductivity or magnetism; quantum effects matter at low temperatures (superfluids). Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: The model is powerful for many thermal properties, but more detailed models of bonding and quantum behaviour are needed (NOS: models have limitations).

items.stem: "Ice packs are more effective than cold water packs of the same mass and temperature for treating sports injuries." Discuss.
